title: The One With The Fake Monica

jokes.text: Calm down. You only have to pay for the stuff you bought.
jokes.setup: Monica is panicking about how much a credit card thief has spent on her card.
jokes.punchline: Chandler deadpans a 'reassurance' that is technically true but completely useless and obtuse — she only pays for HER charges, implying the theft is fine.
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler deadpan logic that sounds helpful but is completely unhelpful. Well-structured and economical. Good character integration — this is quintessentially Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? What is it? Why won't anyone look at me? Oh my God, what is it?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Do I have something on my face? Is it a pimple? Oh no, it's a pimple, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what, don't tell me. I already have plenty of reasons women won't look at me.

jokes.text: Wow, what a geek. They spent $69.95 on a Wonder Mop.
jokes.setup: Everyone is judging the credit card thief as reckless and irresponsible.
jokes.punchline: The 'reckless' purchase is a practical, boring household cleaning item — a Wonder Mop.
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — we expect something decadent; we get a mop. Clean setup-punchline. The specific brand name 'Wonder Mop' adds to the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So how did I do?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: In the dream. How was I? Because I'm gonna need details. Was it a ten? Did I make you cry?

jokes.text: Marcel, stop humping the lamp! Stop humping! Now, Marcel, come back!
jokes.setup: The group is in Monica's apartment when Marcel the monkey begins behaving badly.
jokes.punchline: Marcel is humping the lamp — the image itself is inherently absurd and the frantic scolding escalates the comedy.
jokes.explanation: Broad physical comedy that works on a basic level. The visual of a monkey humping a lamp gets the laugh more from the image than from craft. Functional but not clever.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I had this dream that you were in my wedding.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Was I good?

jokes.text: Well, that's what we said about Joey.
jokes.setup: Ross defends Marcel's humping as 'just a phase.'
jokes.punchline: Chandler casually equates Joey's sexual behavior with the monkey's, implying Joey never outgrew it.
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical callback that characterizes Joey perfectly. The comparison of Joey to a sexually mature monkey is both an insult and deeply in-character for both men. Strong economy — the whole joke is five words.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You were pretty damn good in my dream.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, in my dreams I'm terrible. I'm like, all sweaty and confused, and it's over in like, two seconds.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So basically the same as real life.

jokes.text: Let's just say my Curious George doll is no longer curious.
jokes.setup: Marcel has been humping everything in sight and Rachel is reacting to what he just did.
jokes.punchline: The Curious George doll has presumably been violated; 'no longer curious' is the euphemistic punchline — curiosity = innocence, now gone.
jokes.explanation: Clever wordplay that uses the Curious George character name as a double meaning. 'No longer curious' is an elegant euphemism for deflowerment. Well-constructed and quotable. Slightly less character-specific — any of the female friends could say this.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, I had a dream I was doing it on the table.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Which table?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Our table.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I can never eat there again!

jokes.text: She's living my life, and she's doing it better than me.
jokes.setup: Monica is poring over the credit card thief's purchases with increasing envy.
jokes.punchline: The admission that the thief is somehow living Monica's life MORE authentically than Monica herself is pathetically self-aware.
jokes.explanation: A solid character beat that sets up the episode's A-plot comedically. Monica's self-pitying declaration is funny in its bluntness. More of a premise joke than a standalone punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh wow, that's great. I'm so glad we're all sharing this. Really, this is exactly what I wanted to hear today.

jokes.text: She buys tickets to plays I want to see. She shops at stores that I'm intimidated by the salespeople. She spent $300 on art supplies. / You're not an artist. / Yeah, well, I might be if I had the supplies.
jokes.setup: Monica lists all the aspirational things the thief has done with her card, building to art supplies.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe punctures the fantasy by pointing out Monica isn't an artist; Monica's defense — that she 'might be' with supplies — is delusional and funny.
jokes.explanation: The exchange works because Phoebe's interjection is grounded ('you're not an artist') and Monica's rebuttal is perfectly delusional. Good character work for both.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dream sex? That's not real!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Not real? I was there, Joey. I saw you with her. I can't believe you did this to me.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Chandler, it was a dream!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, so now you're going to lie about it? I was drunk, okay? I wasn't thinking clearly. Besides, you started it!

jokes.text: Oh, it's so late for 'shall we?'
jokes.setup: Monica dramatically asks 'Let's compare, shall we?' while already mid-obsession.
jokes.punchline: Chandler sarcastically notes that the formality of 'shall we' is ludicrous given the conversation has already been happening.
jokes.explanation: A tight, observational quip that's very Chandler — puncturing pretension with minimal words. Good economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God! Look at this one! 'Heavy machinery operator needed.' I'm perfect for this!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, you can barely operate a can opener.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: That's different. That's a can opener. This is heavy machinery. It's basically the same thing, just... heavier.

jokes.text: She's got everything I want, and she doesn't have my mother.
jokes.setup: Monica lists everything the thief has that she doesn't — horseback riding, classes, freedom.
jokes.punchline: The real advantage the thief has is not getting items or experiences — it's not having Monica's overbearing mother.
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — the list builds material envy, then pivots to the one thing no credit card can buy you: freedom from Judy Geller. Strong character integration and earns its laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Can you see me operating the drill press?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh yeah, I can see you. What are you wearing?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Um, overalls and a t-shirt.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Keep going...

jokes.text: Joey Switzerland?
jokes.setup: Joey wants a stage name that's 'more neutral' ethnically — Chandler suggests a country known for neutrality.
jokes.punchline: Switzerland's literal neutrality applied as a surname is absurdist and perfectly logical within its own dumb framework.
jokes.explanation: A tight two-word joke with internal logic. Using Switzerland's geopolitical neutrality as the 'neutral' name is smart wordplay. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I need work because I lost all my massage clients to pirates.

jokes.text: Plus I think it should be Joe. Joey makes me sound like I'm... [holds hand low] ...this big. Which I'm not!
jokes.setup: Joey is arguing for a shorter, more dignified name.
jokes.punchline: He physically demonstrates 'this big' by holding his hand near the floor, suggesting smallness — then defensively insists he is NOT that small, leaving what 'this big' refers to ambiguous and dirty.
jokes.explanation: The visual gag with the hand gesture creates an innuendo that the dialogue alone doesn't fully convey. Joey's earnest defensiveness is perfectly in character. Works better on screen than on the page.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I was giving this guy a massage, right? And he kept saying, 'Oh, that would feel so good if you just did it a little to the left.' So I showed him how to do it himself.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Now he doesn't need me anymore. That's why I lost all my clients!

jokes.text: Joe, Joe, Joe... Stalin?
jokes.setup: Chandler is brainstorming 'Joe' names for Joey's stage name, listing them aloud.
jokes.punchline: He lands on 'Stalin' — the name of one of history's most notorious mass murderers — as a potential stage name.
jokes.explanation: The repeating 'Joe, Joe, Joe' builds rhythm before the absurd punchline. The gap between 'neutral stage name' and 'Soviet dictator' is the comedic engine. Well-structured escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So I was thinking, maybe you'd want to be my secretary? You know, answer phones, file things, organize my desk...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, that sounds great!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, and the best part is, my last secretary just had breast reduction surgery, so she's gonna be way more comfortable now. I mean, she was always complaining about her back pain, and now—you know what? This is weird, right?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, a little.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, I shouldn't have said that.

jokes.text: Joe Stalin. Do I know that name? That sounds familiar. / Well, it does not ring a bell with me.
jokes.setup: Chandler has just suggested 'Joe Stalin' as a stage name — the name of the Soviet dictator.
jokes.punchline: Joey vaguely thinks it rings a bell but can't place it; Chandler claims it doesn't ring a bell for him either — both are comedically ignorant of basic world history.
jokes.explanation: The layered comedy here is rich: Joey half-recognizing it is perfect for his character, but Chandler — who JUST suggested it — also claiming ignorance is the funnier beat. Good character integration for both.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Phoebe, you can't be a secretary. You don't even know what a secretary does.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yes I do. You answer phones, you type things, you file things.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, so you know what a secretary does. But Phoebe, you once thought a woman could get pregnant by sitting on a photocopier.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: That was one time!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Last week you asked me if you could get a disease from a stapler.

jokes.text: Joseph Stalin! / I think you'd remember that!
jokes.setup: After a pause, Joey upgraded 'Joe Stalin' to 'Joseph Stalin,' testing how it sounds.
jokes.punchline: Chandler points out that 'Joseph Stalin' is, if anything, MORE recognizable and memorable — as a historical monster.
jokes.explanation: The escalation to 'Joseph' making it MORE problematic is a well-executed second beat. Chandler's 'you'd think you'd remember that' is a good capper.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh no! A dinosaur emergency! We need a paleontologist stat! What is it, a T-Rex with a boo-boo?

jokes.text: Bye Bye Birdie, starring Joseph Stalin. / Joseph Stalin IS the Fiddler on the Roof.
jokes.setup: The group is riffing on Joey using 'Joseph Stalin' as a stage name.
jokes.punchline: Chandler imagines Broadway marquees with Joseph Stalin's name — the contrast of a genocidal dictator in lighthearted musicals is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The escalation into specific Broadway titles is inspired — 'Fiddler on the Roof' especially lands because of its Jewish cultural resonance against a Soviet dictator who persecuted Jews. High quotability. The running gag peaks here.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, so the beeper is for when Carol goes into labor. I got this vanity number—it spells JIMBO.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: JIMBO?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, JIMBO. It's a great number!

jokes.text: So you can dance with the woman that stole your card?
jokes.setup: Monica announces she's going to tap class where the thief is enrolled.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe cuts right to the absurdity of Monica's plan — she's going to take a dance class to confront a criminal.
jokes.explanation: A functional straight-man observation. Works but isn't clever — just puncturing the obvious absurdity of Monica's plan.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: JIMBO? What kind of name is JIMBO for a beeper number?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Although, I gotta say, it does have a nice ring to it as a baby name.

jokes.text: Go to the post office! I'm sure her picture's up!
jokes.setup: Monica insists she needs to see who this woman is.
jokes.punchline: Chandler suggests the post office where wanted criminals are posted — a more efficient and legally appropriate way to identify a thief.
jokes.explanation: Solid Chandler quip with good economy. The post office wanted-poster reference is a clean comedic pivot.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He's our age...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: ...oh my God, that's so young.

jokes.text: This is madness, I tell you. For the love of God, Monica, don't do it!
jokes.setup: Monica is heading off to the tap class despite friends' protests.
jokes.punchline: Chandler dramatically over-protests in mock-operatic fashion, satirizing movie melodrama.
jokes.explanation: Broad, performative Chandler sarcasm. Works as a button on the scene but not particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, he's a senior? In college?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm cradle robbing!

jokes.text: Thank you. [Monica walks out, taking the over-the-top warning at face value or ignoring it entirely]
jokes.setup: Chandler melodramatically begs Monica not to go to the tap class.
jokes.punchline: Monica simply says 'Thank you' and leaves — treating his absurd protest as a sincere goodbye.
jokes.explanation: The single-word dismissal of Chandler's theatrics is a clean button. Monica's total unfazedness is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He's very mature for his age.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh yeah, and he wears big boy pants.

jokes.text: We're just here to observe. / You don't observe a dance class. You dance a dance class!
jokes.setup: Rachel and Monica slip into tap class hoping to watch and identify the thief without participating.
jokes.punchline: The instructor shuts down the absurd notion that one can 'observe' a dance class — you either dance or you don't.
jokes.explanation: The instructor's correction has a good rhythm — the repetition of 'dance a dance class' vs 'observe a dance class' is well-constructed. Decent quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Can you hear the phone ringing?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, you could always try answering it.

jokes.text: Okay, I'm not getting this! / I'm totally getting it!
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel are attempting tap dancing together.
jokes.punchline: Simultaneous opposite reactions — Rachel struggling while Monica, the more uptight and precise one, immediately excels — reveals character through contrast.
jokes.explanation: The contrast is character-rich — Monica's precision vs Rachel's flailing is funny and true to who they are. Economical.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: He's in a meeting right now.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not in a meeting!

jokes.text: Do you ever just feel like you're so unbelievably uncoordinated? [Rachel to Monica in tap class, unaware Monica is nailing it]
jokes.setup: Rachel is flailing through tap class.
jokes.punchline: She commiserates with Monica, assuming shared incompetence — but Monica is clearly 'totally getting it.'
jokes.explanation: A decent ironic beat that extends the previous joke. Rachel's obliviousness plays well but isn't particularly sharp writing.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You actually have to get to work.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know, I know. Could I BE any more employed?

jokes.text: All right. And my dead mother said you are it! I'm with Rachel.
jokes.setup: The instructor asks everyone to grab a partner; Monica is trying not to get stuck partnerless.
jokes.punchline: Monica uses a childish 'my dead mother said you are it' to avoid the humiliation of being unpaired — invoking a dead parent as a playground shield.
jokes.explanation: Dark and original — invoking a deceased parent as a game-choosing mechanism is unexpected and funny. The desperation of the adult woman using a child's game mechanism in a tap class is great character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God. The fish! Where's the fish?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I haven't even started the fish yet.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh no, the fish is ruined.

jokes.text: Great, it's gym class all over again.
jokes.setup: Monica ends up without a partner and is being singled out by the instructor to come to the front.
jokes.punchline: Monica's self-aware reference to being the last picked / called out in gym class frames her adult humiliation through childhood trauma.
jokes.explanation: A relatable but generic gym-class observation. Works as a beat but isn't particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God, oh my God! Carol's in labor!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? Are you sure?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I got beeped! Look!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, call her back!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, okay.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Hi, is Andre there?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, this is Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I really need a massage.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: This is a personal pager!

jokes.text: Why don't I just take off my clothes and have a nightmare?
jokes.setup: The instructor wants Monica to come dance at the front of the class — maximum public exposure and humiliation.
jokes.punchline: Monica suggests the logical next step: stripping and having a nightmare — the two great anxiety dreams merged with her current reality.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent line. The juxtaposition of the two universal anxiety dreams (public nudity and 'a nightmare' as a distinct experience from waking life) with Monica's actual situation in tap class is clever and relatable. It's original, economical, and captures Monica's particular brand of neurotic self-awareness. One of the episode's best lines.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.line: Hi, is this a massage service?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No! No, this is a paleontology office!

jokes.text: Hi, I'm Mon... / Nana. / Monana? / Yeah. It's Dutch.
jokes.setup: Monica, confronting the thief at dance class, starts to give her real name but panics and changes it mid-word.
jokes.punchline: She accidentally combines 'Monica' and 'Nana' into 'Monana,' then doubles down and claims it's Dutch.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully escalating improv panic joke. The accidental portmanteau 'Monana' is funny enough, but Monica claiming it's Dutch is inspired. The structure is perfect — each response makes things worse, and Monica fully commits to the cover story. High quotability. One of the episode's best beats.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, it's 55-JUMBO, not JIMBO.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, that guy's probably in way better shape than me anyway.

jokes.text: You're kidding. I spent three years in Amsterdam. [Speaks Dutch] / Um, Pennsylvania Dutch.
jokes.setup: Monica claims 'Monana' is Dutch to explain her fake name.
jokes.punchline: The thief turns out to have lived in Amsterdam and speaks actual Dutch to Monica — forcing Monica to clarify she meant 'Pennsylvania Dutch' (a non-Dutch German dialect).
jokes.explanation: The escalation here is masterful — each step tightens the trap. Monica claims 'Dutch,' the thief speaks real Dutch, Monica has to retreat to 'Pennsylvania Dutch' which is not Dutch at all. The structure of this escalating lie is one of the tightest comedic constructions in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, I knew you were going to die.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, I saw it. You were gonna get hit by a truck.

jokes.text: Hey, he beat you!
jokes.setup: Ross reveals Marcel has reached 'sexual maturity' — i.e., is now fully sexually developed.
jokes.punchline: Joey cheerfully congratulates Marcel on beating Chandler's milestone — a callback to the earlier joke equating Joey's sexual behavior with Marcel's.
jokes.explanation: A tight callback to the earlier Chandler joke. Joey congratulating Marcel on sexual maturity is perfectly in character — Joey sees it as a milestone to celebrate and frames Chandler as the comparison bar. Four words, big laugh. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, there's... no, everyone hates you.

jokes.text: I know, I know. One day he's this little thing... and before you know it, he's this little thing... I can't get off my leg.
jokes.setup: Ross is lamenting how fast Marcel has grown up, starting a sentimental 'before you know it' speech.
jokes.punchline: The expected capper — some touching observation about growth — is replaced with 'this little thing I can't get off my leg,' referring to Marcel's humping.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed misdirection — 'this little thing' sets up a sentimental speech and then reveals something anatomically embarrassing. The repeated 'this little thing' structure is elegant. Ross's earnestness makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you should hear what they call him at work now. First it was 'The Chandman', then 'C-Dog', and now... 'Boss Man Bing'.

jokes.text: How do you get a monkey into a zoo? / I know that one!
jokes.setup: Ross asks the group how one gets a monkey placed in a zoo, asking a genuine logistical question.
jokes.punchline: Joey enthusiastically claims to know the answer — treating a sincere question like a riddle he's heard before.
jokes.explanation: Joey thinking a sincere question is a joke/riddle is perfectly in character. The setup is baited well and Joey's certainty is the laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, they're always doing Chandler impressions at work.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more of a statistical analysis processor? Oh. My. God.

jokes.text: No, that's popes into a Volkswagen.
jokes.setup: Joey claims to know how to get a monkey into a zoo, implying a joke punchline is coming.
jokes.punchline: Chandler reveals Joey was thinking of a completely different joke — popes in a Volkswagen — which is itself absurdist and funny.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding joke. The misdirection is layered: we expect Joey to know a monkey-zoo joke, Chandler corrects that he's thinking of 'popes in a Volkswagen' — which is itself a reference to a joke that doesn't exist in any recognizable form, which makes it funnier. The specificity of 'popes into a Volkswagen' (plural popes, a Volkswagen specifically) is inspired absurdism. High quotability and a true standout.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more of a coffee table?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more of a lamp?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more of a fire extinguisher?

jokes.text: But that's two blocks from the beach. It's a total party zoo.
jokes.setup: The Miami zoo is mentioned as a possible placement for Marcel.
jokes.punchline: Ross dismisses Miami as a 'party zoo' — projecting human nightlife concerns onto an animal enclosure.
jokes.explanation: Delightful absurdism — Ross treating zoo culture like college campus selection is funny and very Ross. 'Total party zoo' is an inspired phrase and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I do not sound like that!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more clear?

jokes.text: Are you insane? This woman stole from you! She stole! She's a stealer!
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel reveal they've befriended the woman who stole Monica's credit card rather than reporting her.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's outrage escalates to the tautological — 'She's a stealer!' — which is both technically true and hilariously redundant.
jokes.explanation: The escalation to 'she's a stealer' is mildly amusing in its redundancy but not particularly sharp. Works as a reactive beat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: He literally thought 'gunpoint' was a geographic location

jokes.text: Yeah, which she probably stole from some cheerleader!
jokes.setup: Monica gushes that the thief has an 'amazing spirit.'
jokes.punchline: Chandler suggests the spirit was also stolen — extending the theft metaphor with sharp wit.
jokes.explanation: Excellent quip — extending the theft metaphor to the abstract quality of 'spirit' is clever and well-structured. The cheerleader specificity adds to the funny. Chandler at his best: economical and sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, so the gun is, like, right at your head?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes, Joey, that's what 'gunpoint' means.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh! I thought it was a place! Like, 'gunpoint, New Jersey!' Why would anyone go there?

jokes.text: Take off their hats. / Popes in a Volkswagen! Mm-hm. I love that joke.
jokes.setup: Apparently Joey has been quietly working out the popes/Volkswagen joke and finally arrives at the punchline.
jokes.punchline: Joey triumphantly announces the punchline ('Take off their hats') and Chandler, with satisfaction, names the joke — 'Popes in a Volkswagen' — and expresses love for it.
jokes.explanation: The callback payoff is beautifully delayed and constructed. Joey's been mentally working on this for two scenes. The delivery is perfect — he nails the punchline, Chandler validates it warmly, and 'I love that joke' is the perfect button. The whole running gag pays off here. One of the episode's top moments.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Are you a virgin?

dialogue.speaker: Ethan
dialogue.line: A what?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: A virgin.

dialogue.speaker: Ethan
dialogue.line: Oh! Um, is that like... a Virgo?

jokes.text: We told them we were the Gunnersons in room 615... only to find out the Boston Celtics had the entire sixth floor!
jokes.setup: Rachel is recounting how she and 'Monana' crashed a hotel party.
jokes.punchline: Their fake identity put them on a floor that happened to be occupied by the entire Boston Celtics team — professional basketball players who are very tall and very male.
jokes.explanation: The punchline is the specific wrong floor — the Boston Celtics' floor — which is a good specific detail. Sets up the next beat well.

dialogue.speaker: Ethan
dialogue.line: I've excelled at every level. I'm treating sex like an academic level I haven't reached yet.

jokes.text: So when they caught on to the fact that we're short and have breasts... They threw us out. I was thrown out of a hotel! Me!
jokes.setup: Rachel and Monica tried to crash the Boston Celtics' floor by pretending to belong.
jokes.punchline: Their disguise failed because of basic biological differences; Monica's outrage is the button — 'I was thrown out of a hotel! Me!' — the perfect character reaction for rule-following Monica.
jokes.explanation: 'I was thrown out of a hotel! Me!' is a great character beat — Monica's indignation at rule-breaking when she herself is the offender is rich with irony. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ethan
dialogue.line: I practiced.

jokes.text: Well, you ladies are not the only ones living the dream. I get to go pour coffee for people I don't know. Don't wait up.
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel are excitedly recounting their wild adventure. Chandler is heading to work.
jokes.punchline: Chandler sardonically frames his mundane service-job as an equally aspirational 'dream' — deadpan self-deprecation.
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler sarcasm — framing the mundane as aspirational. 'Don't wait up' is a perfect deadpan exit. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I knew I was attracted to you after our first kiss.

dialogue.speaker: Ethan
dialogue.line: Really? Well, I had a Tic Tac.

jokes.text: There's an open call for Cats. I'm thinking we go down there, sing 'Memories'... and make complete fools of ourselves. What do you say?
jokes.setup: Fake Monica announces tomorrow's plan as though auditioning for a Broadway show is a fun recreational activity.
jokes.punchline: The honest framing — 'make complete fools of ourselves' — as the goal rather than a risk is the inversion. She's pitching embarrassment as the appeal.
jokes.explanation: The self-aware embrace of failure as the plan is a good character moment for Fake Monica and sets up the episode's thematic tension with Monica's fear. Competent writing.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wow, your breath is so fresh!

dialogue.speaker: Ethan
dialogue.line: Thanks, I just had a Tic Tac.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: A Tic Tac? Just one?

jokes.text: Remember who you're dealing with here. I'm not like you. I can't even stand in front of a tap class. / That's because of your Amish background.
jokes.setup: Monica says she's too self-conscious to make a fool of herself publicly.
jokes.punchline: Fake Monica attributes this to Monica's 'Amish background' — a callback to the Pennsylvania Dutch cover story.
jokes.explanation: A good callback that keeps the Pennsylvania Dutch/Amish thread alive. Fake Monica fully accepting and running with the fiction is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He's in high school? Oh my God! That's like... that's like me dating someone in middle school!

jokes.text: Well, you're Pennsylvania Dutch, right? / Right. / Till I bought a blow dryer. Then I was shunned.
jokes.setup: Fake Monica takes the Pennsylvania Dutch/Amish thing further.
jokes.punchline: Monica, fully committed to the lie, has an answer ready: she was shunned for buying a blow dryer — a very Amish-appropriate reason for exile.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the Amish lie is excellent — the blow dryer as the specific device of Monica's excommunication is perfectly chosen (vanity device vs. Amish simplicity). Monica going along with it completely shows character growth within the lie. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ethan
dialogue.line: I'm not a virgin anymore!

jokes.text: Did you ever see Dead Poets Society? / Uh-huh. / I thought that movie was so incredibly... boring!
jokes.setup: Fake Monica references Dead Poets Society as if it's a profound, life-changing film — which is what everyone assumes about it.
jokes.punchline: She found it incredibly boring — the expected adjective is 'inspiring' or 'moving'; 'boring' is the inversion.
jokes.explanation: The setup is excellent — all audience expectations point to 'inspiring.' The sustained pause before 'boring!' works perfectly in delivery. The subsequent logical breakdown ('Kid, wait a year, do some community theater!') is bonus craft.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, so now I'm going to jail! For what, exactly? Dating someone who's slightly younger? I could be arrested for that! They could charge me with... with... 'Contributory Monica-ness'! I'd get twenty years, and I'd have to register as a predator in every state I move to!

jokes.text: I mean, that thing at the end where the kid kills himself because he can't be in the play? What was that? It's like, 'Kid, wait a year. Leave home, do some community theater!'
jokes.setup: Fake Monica is explaining why she found Dead Poets Society boring.
jokes.punchline: She reduces the suicide at the film's climax to a practical problem that could've been solved with community theater — comedically deflating high drama with practical, prosaic advice.
jokes.explanation: Dark but earned — the comedy comes from the character's worldview (pragmatic, life-is-short) reducing tragedy to a solvable inconvenience. 'Do some community theater' is a great specific detail.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm like Demi Moore, except instead of dating younger men, I date men my own age who act younger.

jokes.text: I walked out of there, and I thought: 'Now, that's two hours of my life that I'm never getting back!' And that scared me more than all the other crap I was afraid to do.
jokes.setup: Fake Monica explains her life philosophy emerged from wasting time watching a boring movie.
jokes.punchline: The fear of wasted time — not the fear of failure — is what drove her to stop being afraid. An original, counter-intuitive life philosophy.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely funny and internally consistent character philosophy. The joke works on multiple levels: it's comedy AND it's a real insight about this person. The specificity of the Dead Poets Society framing makes it feel earned rather than abstract.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You're like Joan Collins!

dialogue.speaker: Ethan
dialogue.line: Who's Joan Collins?

jokes.text: Wow. / Then I would definitely not recommend Mrs. Doubtfire.
jokes.setup: Monica is moved by Fake Monica's inspiring philosophy about not wasting time.
jokes.punchline: Fake Monica immediately extends the logic — if Dead Poets Society scared her into action, Mrs. Doubtfire would have the same effect, implying she also wasted time on it.
jokes.explanation: A perfect button on the scene. The pivot from genuine inspiration to a joke about another mediocre movie is excellently timed. 'I would definitely not recommend Mrs. Doubtfire' lands as a great punchline because it reframes the entire preceding speech as a movie-review rant. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, so in this dream, you're not always there?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Sometimes I'd just wake up in the morning and be like, 'What did I miss?'

jokes.text: We didn't get into Scranton. / That was our safety zoo. / They take, like, dogs and cows.
jokes.setup: Ross reveals the Scranton zoo rejected Marcel.
jokes.punchline: Joey reframes Scranton as a 'safety zoo' — like a safety school — and then explains its low standards: dogs and cows.
jokes.explanation: The college-admissions framework applied to zoo placement is funny and very Joey. 'Safety zoo' is an inspired phrase. 'They take, like, dogs and cows' is a perfect extension — farm animals as the zoo equivalent of community college.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, I have a note from my mother.

jokes.text: They take, like, dogs and cows.
jokes.setup: Scranton was dismissed as a safety zoo
jokes.punchline: Ross elaborates that Scranton's zoo is so low-tier it accepts animals that aren't even exotic
jokes.explanation: Good tag on the safety zoo bit. The image of a zoo with just dogs and cows is absurd and funny. Extends the joke but doesn't elevate it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey, little man! You wanna go outside and play with your Power Rangers?

jokes.text: I don't know who this is harder on, me or him. / I'd say that chair's taking the brunt of it.
jokes.setup: Ross is lamenting Marcel's situation emotionally while Marcel is presumably humping a chair.
jokes.punchline: Chandler deadpans that the chair is the real victim — pointing at whatever Marcel is currently assaulting.
jokes.explanation: A tight visual gag — the comedy relies on the audience seeing Marcel in action on the chair. Chandler's economy is perfect: he redirects the emotional question to the physical reality with one deadpan line. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's morphin' time!

jokes.text: You know there already is a Joseph Stalin?
jokes.setup: Presumably Joey has been continuing to consider 'Joseph Stalin' as a stage name.
jokes.punchline: Chandler, long after the conversation, matter-of-factly informs Joey that the name is taken — by a historical mass murderer.
jokes.explanation: The delayed callback is well-executed. Chandler framing the Soviet dictator as a naming-rights issue ('there already IS a Joseph Stalin') is darkly funny. The long gap since the original joke makes its return funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Nobody told me about the office party?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, it was like the most amazing extravaganza! There was dancing and cake and everyone was there... except you.

jokes.text: Phoebe, what do you think a good stage name for me would be? / [Clears throat] Flame Boy!
jokes.setup: Joey, having rejected Joseph Stalin, turns to Phoebe for a stage name suggestion.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's suggestion is 'Flame Boy' — absurd, unprofessional, and nothing like what Joey is looking for.
jokes.explanation: 'Flame Boy' is perfectly Phoebe — enthusiastic, sincere, and completely off-base. The throat-clear before the dramatic reveal adds to the comedy. Strong character integration for both Joey (earnest ask) and Phoebe (unhelpful sincerity).

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I'd love to, but I'm worried people might think you're my date.

jokes.text: Well, it's technically not a zoo per se. It's, uh, more of an interactive wildlife experience.
jokes.setup: Ross asks where exactly the zoo is for Marcel's potential placement.
jokes.punchline: The representative rebrands a substandard zoo as an 'interactive wildlife experience' — classic PR euphemism comedy.
jokes.explanation: A decent satirical beat on marketing language. Works as setup for the more absurd questions to follow.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, the guy needs time to get over the breakup. You can't rush these things. He's gotta watch his stories, eat some ice cream, maybe catch some cartoons in the afternoon.

jokes.text: He can hold a banana, if that's what you mean.
jokes.setup: The zoo rep is asking increasingly odd questions about Marcel's ability to handle 'small objects.'
jokes.punchline: Ross interprets the question charitably — a banana — not realizing the sinister direction the rep is headed.
jokes.explanation: The naive monkey-appropriate answer (banana) against the increasingly dark questioning is a good setup for the payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I think that went really well!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, it doesn't matter. They're gonna make fun of you anyway.

jokes.text: What about a hammer or a small blade?
jokes.setup: The rep has been asking about Marcel's ability to handle objects; Ross innocently mentions a banana.
jokes.punchline: The rep escalates to weapons — hammer, small blade — revealing this is not a conventional zoo.
jokes.explanation: A great escalation beat — the jump from 'small objects' to 'hammer or small blade' is darkly funny. The casualness of the rep's delivery makes it funnier. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: He tried calling himself 'The Chandman,' then 'Chandler the Magnificent,' then just 'Boss Man Cool,' and finally he was down to 'Please Like Me, I'm Desperate.'

jokes.text: If he's up against a jungle cat or an animal with horns... you've got to give the little guy something. Otherwise, it's just cruel!
jokes.setup: Ross is alarmed by the suggestion that Marcel needs a hammer or blade.
jokes.punchline: The rep explains: animal fighting — and frames arming Marcel as the HUMANE option, inverting cruelty entirely.
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy. The reversal — equipping a monkey with a blade is framed as the MERCIFUL option — is brilliant inversion. 'Otherwise, it's just cruel!' is delivered with complete earnestness which is what makes it work. The rep's concern for fairness in animal combat is absurdist gold.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: OK, so if you go into labor, you page me 911.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Ross, 911 is for emergencies.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, isn't this an emergency?

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Yes, but not a 911 emergency. That's for fires, accidents...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Our baby being born isn't a 911 emergency? What if you're in a cab and you go into labor? That's an emergency!

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Just page me a regular number, Ross.

jokes.text: You're making a mistake. San Diego's well and good... but if you give him to me, I'll start him against a blind rabbit... and give you 20 percent of the gate.
jokes.setup: Ross chooses the reputable San Diego Zoo over the shady rep's offer.
jokes.punchline: The rep makes a final pitch: Marcel fighting a blind rabbit, with Ross getting a 20% cut — formalizing the animal-fighting operation with financial incentive.
jokes.explanation: The final pitch escalates the animal-fighting storyline to its logical dark conclusion — and specifying a BLIND rabbit as Marcel's starter opponent is a perfectly horrible detail. The business-deal framing ('20 percent of the gate') makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! I don't need to hear about my cousin's... personal activities!

jokes.text: Are you drunk? / No! [Long pause] I'm lying. I am so drunk!
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel burst in from another adventure. Rachel asks if Monica is drunk.
jokes.punchline: Monica flatly denies it, then immediately recants: 'I'm lying. I am so drunk!' — the self-correction is funnier than the denial.
jokes.explanation: The beat between 'No!' and 'I'm lying' is the joke — Monica's attempt to maintain dignity collapses instantly. Very character-specific: Monica trying to be responsible even while drunk.

dialogue.speaker: Ethan
dialogue.line: I'm not 17 either.

dialogue.speaker: Ethan
dialogue.line: I'm a married congressman.

jokes.text: Water rules!
jokes.setup: Monica stumbles in drunk from crashing an embassy party.
jokes.punchline: In a moment of drunken enthusiasm, Monica hollers 'Water rules!' — a non-sequitur that is deeply funny in its randomness and drunk sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The randomness of 'Water rules!' as the proclamation of a drunk Monica is character-specific comedy — perhaps a reference to what she was drinking, or just a drunk thought. The absurdity is what sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: This is icky.

dialogue.speaker: Ethan
dialogue.line: Icky? We're not children. This is a mature relationship between two consenting adults, and I'm not going to let you reduce it to something icky.

jokes.text: I'm not just the person who needs to fluff the pillows and pay the bills as soon as they come in! You know, when I'm with her, I'm so much more than that! I'm... I'm Monana!
jokes.setup: Ross is telling drunk Monica she's going to lose her job and this 'isn't her.'
jokes.punchline: Monica's declaration of her new identity — 'I'm Monana!' — lands as the drunk, triumphant callback to her fake name, and it's pathetically earnest.
jokes.explanation: A great callback — 'Monana' as Monica's aspirational alter ego, proclaimed drunkenly, is the emotional and comedic peak of her A-plot. 'I'm Monana!' is highly quotable and works both as comedy and character revelation.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, they're not wet anymore. I just... I just like to keep them moist.

jokes.text: Ahem, Monana, it's for you. The credit card people. / They've arrested Monica.
jokes.setup: Monica has just grandly declared herself 'Monana,' the free spirit
jokes.punchline: Immediately, the phone brings news that her real identity has caught up with her — the fake Monica has been arrested
jokes.explanation: The ironic timing of Monica's big Monana declaration being immediately undercut by reality is well-structured. Rachel's deadpan 'Monana, it's for you' followed by the twist is a good beat. The structure is the joke's strength.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more at this office party?

jokes.text: Monica, I started my day by peeing in front of 25 other women... and you're worried about who will take you to the Big Apple Circus?
jokes.setup: Monica is bemoaning her social loss while visiting Fake Monica in jail.
jokes.punchline: Fake Monica puts the self-pity in perspective with a specific, humiliating jail-reality detail: communal toilets.
jokes.explanation: The specificity — '25 other women,' 'peeing' — makes this land harder than a vague jail reference would. The contrast with 'the Big Apple Circus' is perfectly constructed. A strong punchline that reframes Monica's self-pity sharply.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm giving birth!

jokes.text: Well, not worried, you know, just wondering.
jokes.setup: Fake Monica calls Monica out for worrying about circus companions while she's in jail.
jokes.punchline: Monica's semantic retreat — 'not worried, just wondering' — is a perfectly Monica distinction: technically a correction, substantively the same.
jokes.explanation: Extremely Monica — the self-correction that changes nothing is deeply character-specific. Economical and true.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I think I broke my thumb.

jokes.text: I don't know what it is. Maybe it's the Amish thing. / Um, I'm not actually Amish. / Really? Then why are you like that?
jokes.setup: Fake Monica is urging Monica to be less restrained; Monica admits she's not Amish.
jokes.punchline: Fake Monica's response — 'Really? Then why are you like that?' — drops the Amish explanation and replaces it with a direct, more cutting observation about Monica's personality.
jokes.explanation: A great callback payoff — the Amish fiction is finally dropped, and Fake Monica's follow-up question is sharp and funny. 'Then why are you like that?' is a devastating but affectionate line. Good economy and high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait! I need to fix my hair and put on makeup.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, you're in labor!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know, but what if there's cute doctors at the hospital?

jokes.text: You by the door, in or out? / In!
jokes.setup: Monica pauses at the door of the dance studio, seemingly hesitating about whether to commit.
jokes.punchline: When challenged, Monica immediately, decisively shouts 'In!' — her competitive instinct overriding her hesitation.
jokes.explanation: A nice character moment — Monica's can't-back-down instinct kicking in. Economical and character-true.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, we're gonna be there a long time. I'm not sitting in a hospital for hours without snacks.

jokes.text: You by the door, in or out? / In!
jokes.setup: Monica is watching through the door of the dance class, hesitating after her jail visit
jokes.punchline: The teacher's blunt challenge forces Monica's hand — and her immediate 'In!' shows her arc completing
jokes.explanation: A beat that works more for character resolution than comedy, but the teacher's no-nonsense callback to the episode's opening dance scene ('you don't observe') gives it comedic flavor.

jokes.text: You in the back, you're getting it wrong! / At least I'm doing it!
jokes.setup: Monica is dancing (badly) at the back of the class and gets called out by the instructor.
jokes.punchline: Monica fires back with 'At least I'm doing it!' — the thematic point of the episode delivered as a comeback.
jokes.explanation: Monica's 'At least I'm doing it!' works as both character comedy and thematic punctuation. Her defiance getting a laugh in context of her arc is good sitcom craft.

jokes.text: Okay, but don't eat it till you get on the plane.
jokes.setup: Phoebe gives Marcel a poem she wrote for him as a farewell gift.
jokes.punchline: She instructs him not to eat the poem until he's on the plane — treating the monkey as a reader who might eat paper as a separate choice.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Phoebe — her concern is not that the monkey CAN'T read the poem but that he might eat it too early. The specificity of 'till you get on the plane' as if that's when you want to read a poem is delightful.

jokes.text: Okay, bye, champ. There's gonna be a lot of babes in San Diego... but remember, there's also a lot to learn.
jokes.setup: Joey says goodbye to Marcel with a man-to-man speech.
jokes.punchline: Joey's advice to the monkey is the advice of a mentor to a younger player — 'a lot of babes... but also a lot to learn.' The duality of this guidance given to a monkey is perfectly Joey.
jokes.explanation: Joey treating Marcel's San Diego relocation as a college freshman going to party school is brilliant character integration. The 'babes and learning' duality is pure Joey worldview applied absurdly to a monkey. High character specificity.

jokes.text: I don't know what to say, Ross. Uh, it's a monkey. / Just say what you feel, Joey.
jokes.setup: Ross asks Joey to say something meaningful to Marcel before he goes.
jokes.punchline: Joey's blunt acknowledgment — 'it's a monkey' — as the reason he has nothing to say is honest comedy; Ross's earnest 'just say what you feel' is the straight-man escalation.
jokes.explanation: Joey's pragmatic 'it's a monkey' cuts through Ross's sentimentality. The exchange works as a good character contrast joke.

jokes.text: Marcel, I'm hungry. / ROSS: That was good.
jokes.setup: Joey is told to 'say what you feel' to Marcel.
jokes.punchline: He does exactly that — he says what he currently feels, which is hunger. Ross accepts this sincerely as a moving goodbye.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding joke. Joey takes 'say what you feel' literally and reports his current physical state — hunger — as his heartfelt goodbye to the monkey. Ross accepting this as touching ('That was good') is the perfect cap. Exceptional economy, perfect character integration — no one else in the show could deliver this. One of the episode's best jokes, comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor and beyond.

jokes.text: [Ross gives Marcel a banana] It's, uh, just, you know, something to... do on the plane.
jokes.setup: Ross gives Marcel a parting gift — a banana
jokes.punchline: The banana is positioned as a meaningful farewell gift, then Ross sheepishly explains it's 'just something to do on the plane' — acknowledging it's just a banana
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny moment. Ross's emotional investment in Marcel clashing with the reality of giving a monkey a banana as a farewell gift is gently comic. The sheepish explanation is charming character work.

jokes.text: Marcel, would you leave my leg alone? Would you just stop humping me for two seconds? Marc... Would you...? Okay, would you just take him away? Just take him.
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to have a heartfelt one-on-one goodbye with Marcel.
jokes.punchline: Marcel ruins the emotional farewell by humping Ross's leg, destroying the sentiment — Ross goes from 'buddy... this is it...' to 'just take him away.'
jokes.explanation: A perfect structural callback — the humping gag that opens the episode is also the final beat with Marcel. Ross's emotional farewell being demolished by the behavior he couldn't stop is beautifully ironic. The escalation of his exasperation ('would you just stop... would you...') and then abrupt 'just take him' is a great episode closer.

jokes.text: Hi. Uh, I'll be reading for the role of Mercutio. / MAN: Name? / Holden McGroin.
jokes.setup: Joey is auditioning for Romeo and Juliet with a new stage name, building on the episode's running gag about finding the perfect name.
jokes.punchline: 'Holden McGroin' — a phonetic pun on 'holding my groin' — is Joey's chosen stage name, which is both anatomically suggestive and completely absurd.
jokes.explanation: A fantastic episode-closing callback. The entire stage-name subplot pays off with Joey landing on 'Holden McGroin' — a pun that sounds like it could be a real name while being a groin joke. The audition context (Shakespeare, Mercutio) makes it funnier. High quotability. A strong episode button that the audience will remember.

tmdb_overview: When Monica's credit card is stolen, she, along with Phoebe and Rachel, decide to catch the thief. Joey enlists his friends to help him come up with a less ethnic-sounding stage name. And  Ross finds out that Marcel has reached sexual maturity and needs to be with other monkeys.
insight: Early season formula solidifies: 63 jokes in 24 minutes, heavy on character-driven cringe.
